# Adjust contrast

- Route: `/tools/adjust-image-contrast`
- Kind: `tool`
- Category: `photo`
- Slug: `adjust-image-contrast`

## Summary

A Contrast slider that pivots around middle gray, plus Tone and Curves when you want contrast without crushing the ends. (Photo editing)

## Details

Contrast is the distance between the dark and light tones of a photo. In Aperture the Contrast slider in the Light group of the Basic panel stretches every channel away from middle gray by a factor of 2 to the power (contrast / 50): +50 doubles the distance from 0.5, -50 halves it, and 0.5 itself never moves. That is a blunt instrument, which is exactly what you want for a flat scan or a hazy phone photo, and exactly what you do not want when the highlights are already near white. For those cases the same page shows you the Tone group, which adds contrast by pushing Highlights and Shadows apart with luminance weights, and the Curves panel, which lets you draw an S of any steepness through up to 16 points. All three are separate layers and can be masked.
### What it does
- Contrast from -100 to +100 in the Light group: multiplies the distance of each channel from 0.5 by 2 to the power (contrast / 50), so +50 is a factor of 2, +100 a factor of 4, -50 a factor of 0.5.
- Shares a layer with Brightness, which is added first; nudging Brightness a few points moves the pivot in effect, which is how you keep the midtones from darkening when you raise contrast.
- Tone contrast as an alternative: Highlights positive and Shadows negative push the ends apart with smooth luminance weights, and because it rescales the three channels together the hue of every pixel is preserved.
- Curves as the precise alternative: an S through (0.25, 0.2) and (0.75, 0.8) is a mild contrast lift that still reaches both ends of the range, since the curve pins 0 and 1.
- Decreasing contrast (negative values) is a proper fade: -50 maps black to 0.25 and white to 0.75, the look of a matte print, and the result clips nothing.
### How to use it
1. Open the photo: Drop the image. Watch the histogram: a flat photo has a hump in the middle and empty space at both ends.
2. Try the slider first: Raise Contrast toward +30. If the histogram spills past either end before the picture looks right, stop and go to the next step.
3. Shape it with Tone or Curves: Set Contrast back to 0 and use Highlights +30 with Shadows -30, or drag an S on the RGB curve. Both leave the extreme ends in place.
4. Export: Compare with the original, then export at full resolution. The server runs the same multiply, the same weights or the same curve table on the original pixels.
### Supported formats
- Input: JPG, PNG, WebP, GIF, HEIC, HEIF, AVIF, TIFF, BMP
- Output: JPG, PNG, WebP, AVIF, TIFF
- The contrast multiply is applied per pixel in float, so the export shows no banding beyond what the source file and the chosen output quality introduce.
- High positive contrast on an 8-bit source spreads the existing levels apart; at +100 the surviving range of 0.375 to 0.625 holds only 64 source levels, so gradients can band.
### Technical details
- The Light layer computes v = clamp(v + brightness / 200), then v = clamp((v - 0.5) times 2 to the power (contrast / 50) + 0.5), per channel, in sRGB space, with no luminance weighting.
- Factors for common values: +20 is 1.32, +25 is 1.41, +30 is 1.52, +40 is 1.74, +50 is 2.0, +100 is 4.0; -25 is 0.71, -30 is 0.66, -50 is 0.5. Any pixel farther than 0.5 / factor from middle gray clips at +50 or above, so at +50 everything below 0.25 becomes black and everything above 0.75 becomes white.
- Tone contrast: with L the BT.709 luma, Highlights contributes 0.25 times highlights / 100 times smoothstep(0.4, 1, L) to the luma and Shadows 0.25 times shadows / 100 times (1 - smoothstep(0, 0.6, L)); the new luma over the old scales R, G and B, so the maximum shift of one slider at full strength is a quarter of the range.
- Curves build a 256-entry table from a monotone cubic through your points, so an S can never reverse tones. The table is sampled per channel first (Red, Green, Blue curves) and then by the RGB master curve.
- The preview is drawn on your GPU (WebGL2) from a 1920 px copy; the exported file is rendered on our server from the original at full resolution with the same formulas, and the two agree within a small documented tolerance (a few 8-bit levels at most; grain is exact). Contrast, Tone and Curves are per-pixel, so they are among the operations that match to the level.
- Switching the Light layer blend to Luminosity applies only the luma shift and leaves chroma alone, which stops strongly colored pixels from shifting hue when one channel clips before the others.
### When not to use it
When a photo looks flat because of haze or glare rather than a narrow tonal range, Dehaze in the Detail panel is a better fit because it subtracts an estimated veil based on the local dark channel instead of stretching every tone. When a photo looks flat because it is simply dark, raise the exposure first; contrast on top of darkness only makes the shadows blockier. And if one side of the histogram is already clipped, no contrast slider can recover it, so lower Highlights or Whites before you touch Contrast.
### Use cases
- Hazy landscape: Contrast +30 with Brightness -5 returns the depth; if the sky clips, use Dehaze +40 from the Detail panel instead, which works from the darkest channel in each 15 x 15 neighborhood rather than stretching everything.
- Flat scanned document or print: Contrast +40 then Levels with Input black at 0.08 and Input white at 0.92 snaps the paper to white and the ink to black.
- Harsh midday portrait: Contrast -20 on a brush-masked layer over the face softens the light on the skin while the background keeps its punch.
- Matte film look: Contrast -35 lifts black to 0.19 and drops white to 0.81, then Split toning adds a warm highlight and a cool shadow to finish the look.
### FAQ
Q: Why does middle gray not change when I move Contrast?
A: Because the formula pivots on 0.5: the value is subtracted, multiplied and added back, so (0.5 - 0.5) times any factor is still 0. Everything lighter moves toward white and everything darker moves toward black by the same proportion.
Q: At what setting does the Contrast slider start clipping?
A: Any positive value clips something if the photo already reaches both ends. At +25 (factor 1.41) tones below 0.146 or above 0.854 clip; at +50 (factor 2) the thresholds are 0.25 and 0.75; at +100 (factor 4) only 0.375 to 0.625 survives. If the histogram touches an edge, use Tone or Curves instead.
Q: Should I use Contrast or Clarity?
A: Contrast is global and tonal. Clarity in the Detail panel is a local contrast: it adds the difference between a pixel and a blurred copy of its neighborhood, weighted toward the midtones. Clarity makes textures pop without moving the histogram ends; Contrast moves the whole distribution.
Q: How do I reduce contrast without the photo looking washed out?
A: Use a small negative Contrast such as -15, then bring the blacks back with Tone Blacks -20 so the darkest tones return to the floor. The result keeps a solid black point with compressed midtones, which reads as soft rather than foggy.
Q: Does the slider change saturation?
A: Yes, slightly, because it works per channel in sRGB: a color with channels 200, 120, 80 at +30 becomes 237, 116, 56, and the gap between the channels has grown. Set the layer blend to Luminosity if you want the tonal change without the color change.
Q: What is the difference between Contrast and Levels?
A: Levels picks explicit input black and white points and a midtone gamma, so you decide exactly which tones become 0 and 1. Contrast applies one symmetric factor around 0.5. Levels is better when the histogram is lopsided; Contrast is faster when it is centered.
